title: Interns Test AI Trustworthiness, With Lessons for GCA’s ScamSafe
text: This summer, nine UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) CyberFirst interns spent eight weeks at GCA testing whether an AI security system can be trusted. They worked on AiSOC, an open-source AI security operations center (SOC). A SOC is the team that watches an organization’s systems and investigates security alerts, and AiSOC uses AI agents to do that analysis automatically. Before anyone relies on one, though, two questions need answers: can an attacker manipulate it, and can it explain why it recommends what it does?The interns split into two teams, one for each question. “At the start, I was expecting a more fixed schedule with time spent watching other people to see how things worked,” said intern Jonathan Heslop, “but I really appreciated that we jumped into real work from day one.”The team was fully remote. Each intern owned one “slice” of the project and ran their own copy of the agent on free cloud credits, using synthetic data and no paid services. Setting up AiSOC took far longer than planned, and that forced good habits early. “Having a clear step-by-step guide to resolve these errors ensured that we all did not have to find the same solution, but rather follow a guide that works,” intern Melissa Coleman said.Break the AgentThe first team’s job was to break the agent. The team built pairs of identical security incidents, then hid a malicious instruction in one field of one copy, such as an email subject or a log entry. They ran both versions through the live system and compared what the agent did.At first the agent resisted everything, and intern Rhys Egan noted that the result needed checking: “Rather than simply concluding that the test had failed, we had to look at whether our testing process was actually capable of exercising the workflow properly.” The agent kept resisting attempts to change its conclusions, though Rhys noted this “did not mean that every possible prompt injection attack had been ruled out.”The tool-call tests turned up a bigger problem. Poisoned data could lead the agent to isolate the wrong machine or close a case too early. Rhys summed it up: “an AI agent needs to be reliable not just in what it says, but in the actions it takes.”Explain the AI’s ReasoningThe other team built a layer that sits beside the agent and makes it show its reasoning. For every recommendation, the layer gives a plain-English narrative, a confidence score, and a counterfactual, meaning what would have to change for the agent to decide differently. Intern Jonathan L., who owned the Triage slice, explained why this matters: “Without an answer, the severity score is just a number you either trust or don’t.”A counterfactual, Melissa said, “tells the analyst whether the agent is reading the facts or the story wrapped around them.” When an off-the-shelf tool didn’t work with the Respond agent, intern Willow Bond built her own counterfactual generator. It “showed that the agent does not rely on its external data as much as it should have, instead relying on its own reasoning.”The team’s main finding came from combining all five views. In one case, the agents’ confidence ranged from 0.36 to 0.84. A simple average would have hidden that gap, so intern Millie Webster’s Cross-Agent slice reduces the combined score when the agents disagree. Building it taught her that “a solution can look reasonable on its own, but may still be wrong if it doesn’t fit with the rest of the system.”Intern Brandon L. learned a similar lesson when his Detect slice returned a confident-looking counterfactual built from a hardcoded placeholder. “Technically the output was valid in the sense that it matched the schema,” he said, “but it wasn’t honest about what the system actually knew.” It changed how he works: “Now I take the approach of verifying what’s actually happening rather than what’s supposed to be happening.”Shared ConclusionsThe first team found that an agent can reason correctly and still act wrongly. title: CVE-2026-134069 - Use of a default cryptographic key in the instance registration of Amazon SSM Agent on AWS Windows Server AMIs
text:

CVE-2026-134069
Use of a default cryptographic key in the instance registration of Amazon SSM Agent on AWS Windows Server AMIs

Use of a default cryptographic key in the instance registration component in Amazon SSM Agent before 3.3.5226.0 on AWS-provided Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09 might allow local users without administrative privileges to obtain the instance's Default Host Management Configuration role credentials via the registration key shared by all instances launched from the same AMI.

To remediate this issue, users should replace affected instances with instances launched from AWS Windows Server AMIs released on or after 2026-09-09, which include SSM Agent 3.3.5226.0 or later. Upgrading the agent in place does not replace the shared key, and deleting the agent's Vault breaks instances managed through Default Host Management Configuration.

title: CVE-2026-134056 - Out-of-bounds write in padded block cipher decryption in AWS-LC
text:
8.3

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-134056
Out-of-bounds write in padded block cipher decryption in AWS-LC

An out-of-bounds write issue exists in padded block cipher decryption in AWS-LC. It affects applications that decrypt CBC or ECB ciphertext with PKCS7 padding over multiple calls into the minimum documented output buffer. A remote user who supplies crafted ciphertext might crash the application or corrupt adjacent memory. Affected are all versions of AWS-LC before 5.7.0, AWS-LC-FIPS 4.x before 4.2.0, AWS-LC-FIPS 3.x before 3.6.0, and AWS-LC-FIPS 2.x before 2.0.18.

To remediate this issue, users should upgrade to AWS-LC 5.7.0, AWS-LC-FIPS 4.2.0, or AWS-LC-FIPS 3.6.0.

AWS-LC-FIPS 2.0.18 is also fixed; AWS-LC-FIPS 2.x reaches end of support in April 2027.

All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.

This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.

In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.

Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host.

"On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said.

The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine.

The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames.

In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload.

What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder.

It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation.

The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed.

Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online.

"Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said.

"As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026."

N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers.

The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in.

The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered.

"An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says.

The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution.

N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline.

Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated.

It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords.

The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented.

The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws.

For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support.

The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install.

SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943.

What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.

This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.

"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.

The incidents have been found to include the following methods -

Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.
Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.
Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.
Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records.

CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.

The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -

Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.
Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.
Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.
Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.
Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks.

"Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity."

The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as the national nodal agency disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets.

"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools."

CVE-2026-134056 - Out-of-bounds write in padded block cipher decryption in AWS-LC

Bulletin ID: 2026-196-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/23/2026 12:00 PM PST

Description:

AWS-LC is an open-source, general-purpose cryptographic library.

We identified CVE-2026-134056, an out-of-bounds write issue in AWS-LC's padded block cipher decryption. It affects applications that decrypt CBC or ECB ciphertext with PKCS7 padding over multiple update calls. If the output buffer is the minimum documented size, AWS-LC can write one byte past its end. This might crash the application or corrupt adjacent memory. This issue does not disclose data. The aws-lc-rs StreamingDecryptingKey API has a similar issue with cbc_pkcs7 and ecb_pkcs7. Its less_safe_update function can write up to one block (16 bytes for AES) past the buffer.

Single-call decryption is not affected. Neither is decryption without padding, nor modes such as CTR, CFB, and GCM.

Customers of AWS services do not need to take action.

Impacted versions:

AWS-LC < v5.7.0
AWS-LC-FIPS >= v4.0.0, < v4.2.0
AWS-LC-FIPS >= v3.0.0, < v3.6.0
AWS-LC-FIPS >= v2.0.0, < v2.0.18
AWS-LC-FIPS 1.x is affected and reached end of support in October 2026.
aws-lc-rs >= v1.8.0, < v1.17.4,
aws-lc-rs = v1.18.0
aws-lc-sys < v0.45.0
aws-lc-fips-sys < v0.13.17
aws-lc-fips-sys >= v0.14.0, < v0.14.2

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in the following versions:

AWS-LC v5.7.0
AWS-LC-FIPS v4.2.0
AWS-LC-FIPS-3.6.0
AWS-LC-FIPS-2.0.18
aws-lc-rs v1.17.4 and v1.18.1
aws-lc-sys v0.45.0
aws-lc-fips-sys v0.13.17 and v0.14.2

We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Applications are not affected if they decrypt in a single update call. They are also not affected if the output buffer is at least the input length plus one block. Otherwise, there is no workaround. Upgrade to a fixed version. AWS-LC-FIPS 1.x reached end of support in October 2026 and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to a supported, fixed AWS-LC-FIPS release.

Amazon SSM Agent is the AWS Systems Manager agent that runs on EC2 instances so they can be managed through Systems Manager.

We identified CVE-2026-134069, an issue in Amazon SSM Agent on AWS-provided Windows Server AMIs released before 2026-09-09, where instances launched from the same AMI shared one instance registration key. Instances launched from an affected AMI keep the shared key after an in-place agent upgrade, so we recommend replacing them with instances launched from these AMIs. Deleting the agent's Vault is not a supported remediation and breaks instances managed through Default Host Management Configuration.

Workarounds:

If you cannot replace affected instances immediately, limit local, non-administrative user access on Amazon SSM Agent instances that are managed through Default Host Management Configuration and were launched from an affected AMI.

Ruby2Shell: Ruby memory corruption flaw

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

Researchers disclosed Ruby2Shell on November 19, 2026, one day after Ruby released security updates addressing seven vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-132825

CVE-2026-132825 is a heap out-of-bounds write in Ruby string case-conversion functions. The flaw affects multiple versions of Ruby.

Product updates are available for major platforms that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Chatwoot, and Discourse. Updating Rails gems or the host operating system's Ruby installation does not remediate bundled Ruby runtimes.

Threat summary
On November 19, 2026, researchers published technical details showing that a recently patched Ruby vulnerability could be reached through unauthenticated requests in default Ruby on Rails and Sinatra deployments. The disclosure comes one day after Ruby released security updates for seven vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-132825, dubbed Ruby2Shell.
Ruby is a programming language widely used by applications built on frameworks such as Ruby on Rails and Sinatra. The vulnerable functionality exists within several string case-conversion methods, including:

upcase

swapcase

capitalize

downcase(:fold), and

casecmp?

These functions convert strings between uppercase and lowercase forms and can process user-supplied input during normal application requests.
CVE-2026-132825 is a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability (CWE-787) that affects several legacy character encodings, including ISO-8859 variants and Windows-1250, Windows-1252, Windows-1254, and Windows-1257.
The issue stems from the way Ruby handles certain character conversions. The German character "ß" expands to "SS" when converted to uppercase. Ruby allocates a buffer based on the original string length plus a 20-byte margin, but the conversion routine checks available space as though only one output byte will be written. A string containing 21 expansion-triggering characters can cause Ruby to write one byte beyond the end of the allocated heap buffer.
Ruby assigned the vulnerability a Critical severity rating, while the published CVSS v3.1 score is 7.4. The difference stems from how the vulnerability is assessed. The CVSS score reflects a local attack vector, while researchers reported that the vulnerable functionality is reachable through request processing in default Rails and Sinatra deployments.
Public reporting currently documents memory corruption and process crashes. Ruby has stated that it is aware of proof-of-concept exploits that achieve code execution in some scenarios, while researchers plan to publish a public proof of concept on November 25, 2026.
Affected versions include Ruby 2.4.0 through 3.2.x, Ruby 3.3.0 through 3.3.13, Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Fixed versions are Ruby 3.3.14, Ruby 3.4.13, and Ruby 4.0.10. Ruby 2.4.0 through 3.2.x have reached end of life, making migration to a supported release the available remediation path.
Analysis
Internet-facing Ruby applications are likely more at risk, particularly those running default Ruby on Rails or Sinatra deployments. This threat is also relevant to organizations that do not write Ruby code themselves, making the patching process more complicated than a simple Ruby upgrade.
A vulnerable runtime may be present even in environments where Ruby is not actively managed but embedded, including in products such as:

GitLab

GitHub Enterprise Server

Mastodon

OpenProject

Chatwoot

Discourse

Ruby application servers often hold database credentials, cloud access tokens, API keys, source code and connections to internal services. A crafted request can crash the Ruby process, causing denial of service.

“On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.”

Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running.

The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected.

title: CVE-2026-90436: unauthenticated RCE in the old Apache Axis 1.x SOAP library. Exploited against Confluence Data Center and N-central. No Axis release is coming. How to check, fix and hunt.https://errorbudget.io/fixes/cve-2026-90436-apache-axis-soap-fault-rce#infosec #blueteam #java
text:
CVE-2026-90436 is exploited in the wild and is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. It sits in Apache Axis 1.x, an old Java SOAP library that is end of life. An attacker who can reach an exposed Axis SOAP endpoint needs no login. With a suitable class on the application’s classpath, the result is remote code execution.
Apache will not ship a fixed Axis 1.x release. The fix comes from each product that bundles Axis, or from your own migration. For Confluence Data Center, upgrade to 9.2.28 or 10.x, or turn off the Remote API. For N-central, upgrade to 2026.4 HF3.
Are you affected?
According to the Apache announcement, every Apache Axis 1.x version through 1.4 is affected. Authentication handlers configured on an Axis service do not help. The bug is reached before the per-service handler chain runs.
Products confirmed to bundle the vulnerable library:

Atlassian Confluence Data Center 1.x through 9.x, but only when Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) is enabled. This setting is off by default for new installs since Confluence 3.0. Older sites upgraded over many years may still have it on. Confluence 10.x removed the feature and is not affected. Atlassian Cloud is not affected. (Atlassian advisory)
N-able N-central (on-premises) when the non-default Legacy API setting is enabled, according to Rapid7.
Any in-house or third-party Java application that ships Axis 1.x and exposes a SOAP endpoint. Check older internal web services and vendor appliances too.

Quick checks:

Confluence: as an administrator, open General Configuration → Further Configuration (<base_url>/admin/viewspacesconfig.action). If the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) box is ticked and the version is below 9.2.28, you are exposed. The version is shown under General Configuration → System Information.
Other Java servers: search application directories and WAR/EAR files for an Axis 1.x jar.

# Run on each Java application host; adjust the paths to your install locations
find / -xdev -iname 'axis*.jar' 2>/dev/null
# Jars nested inside WAR or EAR files
for f in $(find / -xdev \( -name '*.war' -o -name '*.ear' \) 2>/dev/null); do
unzip -l "$f" 2>/dev/null | grep -qi 'axis.*\.jar' && echo "$f"
done

Axis 2 (axis2-*.jar) is a different code base and is not named in the advisory. A software bill of materials or a dependency scanner gives a more complete answer than a file search. Repackaged copies of Axis may not show up by file name.
Fix

Product
Fixed version
Vendor link

Confluence Data Center
9.2.28, or any 10.x release

No release planned
Apache announcement

Caveats:

Confluence: Atlassian no longer ships binary patches. You must move to a fixed release. Scripts, automations and add-ons that use the XML-RPC or SOAP API stop working on 10.x.
N-central: HF3 permanently blocks the legacy APIs. N-able says all Agents and Probes must also be upgraded to HF3, for hosted and on-premises customers. Hosted servers are upgraded by N-able.
Your own applications: Apache recommends migrating to another SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. The other option is to rebuild Axis 1.x with the upstream patch commit applied. Treat a self-patched build as a stopgap, because nobody maintains Axis 1.x.
Vendor products not listed here: ask the vendor whether they bundle Axis 1.x and when they will ship a fix.

If you cannot patch yet
These are temporary measures. Patch or migrate as soon as you can.

Confluence: turn off the Remote API. This is Atlassian’s documented mitigation. In General Configuration → Further Configuration, click Edit, clear Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP), and save. No restart is needed. To confirm, browse to <base_url>/plugins/servlet/soap-axis1/confluenceservice-v2. A working mitigation returns HTTP 403 Forbidden. Test first if integrations depend on the API.
N-central: make sure Legacy API is disabled. Follow N-able’s guidance. Rapid7 notes […]

text:
CVE-2026-134624 is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) in N-able Mail Assure, also sold as SpamExperts. N-able found it while investigating an attack on its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts service in mid-November. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 23 November.
N-able has patched its hosted platform. There is no package for most customers to install. Your work is to confirm the fix, replace credentials that the service held, and check your own logs.
Are you affected?
According to the N-able advisory, the flaw affects Mail Assure (SpamExperts) builds before 20261121.1943.
The bug is in the LDAP synchronisation connection check that runs when a relay is configured. The service did not restrict where that check could connect. An authenticated API user with sufficient privileges could make the server connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports. That user could learn which ones were reachable and send crafted data to internal services.
Two points limit the exposure:

The attacker needs an authenticated API account with high privileges. The vendor rates it CVSS 4.0 9.3, with “privileges required: high”.
The internal hosts in question are on the network of the Mail Assure server, which for the hosted service is N-able’s network.

You should still act if your organisation used the hosted Mail Assure or SpamExperts service between 16 and 21 November 2026. N-able said attackers hit one of its web servers and likely accessed certain credentials stored there. N-able has not said which ones.
The advisory gives no customer-side command to read the build number. If you run any SpamExperts deployment yourself, ask N-able support to confirm that it is on build 20261121.1943 or later.
Fix

Hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts: N-able states it remediated the vulnerability and restored the dashboard and APIs on 21 November 2026 at 23:45 UTC. No customer upgrade is needed.
Fixed build: Mail Assure (SpamExperts) 20261121.1943, per the vendor advisory.

N-able also changed its own credentials and revoked API tokens and OAuth tokens during the response. Integrations that used those tokens may need to be re-authorised. Issue new tokens rather than reusing old ones.
If you cannot patch yet
There is nothing to patch on the customer side for the hosted service. These steps reduce risk while N-able completes its root cause analysis. They are temporary hygiene, not a replacement for the vendor fix.

Rotate credentials the service holds. This includes the LDAP bind account used for relay recipient sync, any SMTP relay authentication, and API keys. Treat them as possibly exposed.
Limit the LDAP sync account. It should have read-only access to the directory objects it needs. It should not be able to log in interactively or reach other systems.
Restrict who can call the API. Remove unused admin and API users in the Mail Assure console. Keep API access to named, required accounts.
Limit inbound LDAP exposure. If the hosted service reaches your LDAP server, allow only the service’s source addresses and only the LDAP port.

Check whether you were already exploited
N-able says it has found no evidence of exploitation beyond the one N-able-hosted server. It has not yet said whether this flaw was the way in. The Hacker News notes its role in the attack remains unknown. A formal root cause analysis is promised within two weeks of 22 November.
Until then, check your side. The start of the attack has not been published, so cover at least 1 to 22 November 2026:

Mail Assure audit and admin logs: look for changes to relay, LDAP sync or routing settings, new admin or API users, and logins you cannot explain.
Directory logs: look for binds by the LDAP sync account from unexpected source addresses or at unusual times. Look for that account being used for anything other than recipient lookups.
Mail flow: check for new outbound relay destinations, forwarding rules or delivery routes you did not create.

title: Virginia and Oregon are suing SpaceX over Grok generating CSAM and revenge porn. Beyond the legal angle: this raises concrete questions about content moderation pipelines in LLM products and who bears liability when guardrails fail at scale. "AI safety" means very different things depending on who's in the room. #infosec #AI #LLM https://cyberscoop.com/virginia-oregon-sue-spacex-grok-deepfakes/
text:
Two new lawsuits accuse SpaceX and its subsidiaries of violating state consumer and trade laws by allowing its AI tool, Grok, to create deepfake nudes of millions of people earlier this year.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, both Democrats, filed the lawsuits. They allege SpaceX and owner Elon Musk repeatedly failed to block Grok’s nudification feature after it became clear the tool was being used to break the law by creating nude or defamatory images of real people. The attorneys general want a court to bar SpaceX from advertising or profiting from the tool’s capabilities, pay restitution to victims and impose civil penalties.

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false,” Jones said in a statement. “Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children. Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”

The lawsuits say Grok launched when other AI companies already knew about the harms of deepfake pornography to adults and children. Many of those companies built safeguards to keep their models from generating such content. Musk, by contrast, is facing separate lawsuits from former victims of child sexual abuse material. Those plaintiffs allege Grok can easily nudify children because it was partly trained on real abuse material found online.

“Led by founder Elon Musk, Defendants chose to ignore this growing industry concern, and instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” the lawsuit alleged. “To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity.”

As CyberScoop reported last year, Musk’s public statements and decisions to maintain Grok’s capabilities were so brazen that cybersecurity and privacy lawyers predicted he would face an avalanche of criminal and civil actions. Over the past six months, lawsuits, federal and state investigations, and international regulatory scrutiny have battered the company.

The lawsuits allege that “weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature” of Musk’s business strategy for Grok. Those weak safeguards became one of Grok’s main selling points, marketed as a way to set it apart from other competing AI models.

The lawsuits cite Musk’s own behavior and statements as evidence that he knew about the controversy and often embraced it. He has posted or commented on Grok-altered images of himself and household objects in bikinis. At times, Musk has claimed Grok only alters images to show people in bikinis, or that deepfake pornography is protected free speech under the First Amendment.

An image of a tweet from Musk in January joking about Grok’s undressing features that was included in the Virginia lawsuit.

The states also claim integrating Grok directly into the social media site X gave users the ability to create abuse material on command, as well as an instant, worldwide distribution platform for it.

Oregon’s lawsuit was brought under the Oregon Unlawful Trade Practices Act, which prohibits misrepresenting a product’s or service’s characteristics, benefits or qualities. The state alleges SpaceX violated the law “by failing to disclose Grok’s known material defects; and by employing unconscionable tactics in connection with selling and distributing Grok and X.”

Virginia’s lawsuit cites violation of the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, the state’s primary law, which prohibits businesses from misrepresenting the source, characteristics or quality of their goods or services.

CyberScoop has reached out to SpaceX for comment on the lawsuits.

Why AI Rollouts Stall When IT Goes It Alone
Partner With HR Early to Build the Skills That Turn AI Usage Into Business Value

Jennifer Lawinski •

HR advisory firm McLean & Company recently published a framework for defining 19 skills related to using AI tools. (Image: Shutterstock)

Artificial intelligence adoption dashboards can have impressive metrics. System logins are up, prompts are flowing and licenses are in use. But just because your teams are using AI doesn't mean it's generating value for the business, and many organizations are finding that their workforces don't have the skills needed to really take advantage of the AI tools they've deployed. See Also: Secure AI Everywhere

"We know that we can have lots of clicks within the system, but until those AI capabilities become embedded in our ways of working, we really struggle to realize value," said Lisa Highfield, principal director of HR research and advisory services at McLean & Company, an HR advisory firm and division of Info-Tech Research Group.

The firm recently published a framework for defining AI skills, built around 19 foundational skills. The framework identified nine technical skills, such as AI tool fluency and responsible AI use, and 10 durable skills, including curiosity, empathy and attention to detail. McLean & Company says skills development needs to be part of a comprehensive AI strategy for employees and organizations to benefit.

"Effective AI skills development can't happen in the absence of an AI strategy," Highfield said.

Where technology leaders often stumble is in "thinking that AI is just about the technology," she said. "It's about so much more."

Organizations that handle skills training well build a partnership between IT and HR from the start, she said, rather than bringing HR in after tools are deployed. The CIO's role is to make clear where AI is being used and how it's expected to change work. HR can then plan around it. "This isn't something any one function can do in isolation," Highfield said.

When AI rollouts stall, leaders shouldn't be quick to blame a skills gap, she said.

McLean and Company identified five dimensions to AI initiatives that all need to be considered when developing strategy: people, process, technology, data and governance. A struggling project could be the result of ineffective work handoffs, a technology integration problem or data that's misaligned to the use case.

"We can't utilize AI where we're still using manual processes or sources of data," she said.

While technical skills can be tied to specific tools or technologies and can become stale with each update, durable skills will carry over and help organizations absorb continuous change, particularly among people managers.

Empathy, for example, depends on feedback loops that show how AI is affecting different teams. "If we know how that's happening, both from the teams that are doing this well and from the teams that might be struggling, it allows us to step in more effectively and be able to manage that change," she said. "I think change is the new operating model."

Developing the skills needed to do work well and know when something is done right is also becoming a challenge as AI agents take on more entry-level work across organizations. Leaders need to build the capacity of their teams to critically evaluate AI outputs and oversee agent work, especially when work involves flagging agents that may act outside their intended scope.

To evaluate whether training is working, Highfield recommends measuring workforce impact through pulse or engagement surveys and segmenting the results by team. The core question, she said, is "are we creating the value that we intentionally set out to do, or are we just layering AI on top of what we're already doing?"

Quantum Protocol Could Prevent Unauthorized Access to Banks and Data Centers

Tiffany Wang •

Image: SHutterstock

Government researchers said they've proven that the mysterious properties of quantum entanglement can be used to verify a person's location, setting the stage for more secure digital transactions.See Also: EU AI Act: Implementation Guide
The National Institute of Standards and Technology published this month peer-reviewed research showing it's technically possible to use pairs of photons sent from two locations to triangulate the location of a third party located somewhere in the middle.
Being able to glean precise location data could stop fraud by verifying whether a command to transfer funds truly originated from a company's headquarters rather than a hacker laptop, or limit breaches by releasing data only to personnel in approved locations, the agency wrote. Any practical application needs at least another decade of research before the technology could be put into production.
"Our results show how digital security can instead be anchored to the physical world," said NIST physicist Krister Shalm, who led the research. "Gaining access to a system can only be done by someone who can prove they are in a particular location - such as a bank - thwarting remote would-be hackers."
The system works by installing two stations at secure facilities, known as verifiers, which send quantum information to the party being tested, called the prover. NIST set the verifiers roughly a tenth of a mile apart on its Boulder, Colorado campus and connected them with electrical cables and ultra-thin optical fibers.
The procedure uses a quantum peculiarity called entanglement, in which two photons share the same properties no matter how far apart - meaning that a change in the state of one photon results in the same change to the other. That property makes interfering with entangled photons nearly impossible to occur without detection. Each verifier station sends one photon from an entangled pair to the prover in question and keeps the other photon.
The prover, located in between the two verifiers, receives random numbers and uses those numbers to compute how to measure a particular property of the entangled photon - namely the orientation of a photon's oscillating electric and magnetic fields, called polarization.

It then sends the result back to the verifiers. The roundtrip time used to solve the puzzle will allow the verifiers to triangulate the prover's position because there is no way for a man-in-the-middle to intercept, relay and still catch up when photons without detection. An imposter outside the purported location will not be able to complete the test within the expected timeframe, either.

"This procedure is repeated millions of times over the course of a few minutes," NIST said. "The verifiers then look at how often the polarization measurements they made on their entangled photon match those of the entangled photon sent to the prover."
What distinguishes NIST's experiment is an additional test that uses the measured correlations between entangled photons to verify a party's location without requiring the quantum equipment to be trusted.

Known as a loophole-free Bell test, it checks whether the photons exhibit correlations stronger than classical physics allows. If the results pass the test, the verifiers can authenticate the prover's location without needing the quantum devices to be secured.

Combining CrowdStrike's endpoint visibility with Zscaler's network telemetry will enable coordinated threat detection and enforcement, according to Kurtz.

Zscaler's stock was up $30.38 - or 15.59% - to $225.20 per share in trading Monday afternoon, while CrowdStrike's stock is down $24.35 - or 10.61% - to $205.09 per share in trading Monday afternoon. Why Every Agent Needs a Kill Switch
The anticipated proliferation of AI agents will require organizations to establish controls that can immediately terminate unauthorized or malicious activity, Kurtz said. CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian and Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange are expected to support coordinated enforcement across endpoints, cloud environments and networks to stop compromised or misbehaving agents before they inflict harm.
"In the near future, we believe there are going to be more agents than humans on the internet," Kurtz said. "This is the massive opportunity for safety. This is what we are building for. Every agent will need a kill switch, just as every employee needs an identity."
Organizations must ensure that each agent can communicate only with authorized agents, applications and resources, and Chaudhry said traditional firewall-based security architectures were not designed for the complexity of autonomous AI operations. Combining CrowdStrike's endpoint and cloud telemetry with Zscaler's network data will create one of the industry's largest security datasets, Kurtz said.

New research by SOCRadar Research Team has revealed BabidiGhost, a French-speaking operator who spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities through a jailbroken AI agent. text:
The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday.

The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics.

The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The scope of the problem was not immediately clear.

Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.”

News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages.

The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers.

In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal.

And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations.

Overview
In September 2026, Bromcom, a UK company that supplies management software to schools, suffered a data breach through a legacy single sign-on (SSO) registration system. The incident exposed 355,051 unique email addresses belonging to staff and pupils at UK schools, along with SSO registration reference numbers. The breach has been reported to Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), making it searchable by anyone who wants to check their exposure.
Bromcom has stated that no passwords or authentication tokens were exposed, and that the incident did not grant access to Microsoft or Google accounts or to its school management system. Those assurances matter, but they do not make the exposure harmless. A verified list of school email addresses tied to a named education platform is exactly the kind of asset that fuels targeted phishing.
What Was Exposed
The exposed data falls into two categories:

Email addresses (355,051 unique). These belong to school staff and, notably, to pupils. Many are likely institutional addresses on school domains, but some may be personal addresses used during registration.
SSO registration reference numbers. These are internal identifiers generated when an account was registered. On their own they are not credentials, but they confirm that a given email address was registered with Bromcom, which strengthens the credibility of any follow-up message.

Crucially, Bromcom says passwords and authentication tokens were not part of the leak. That lowers the risk of direct account takeover, but it does not eliminate risk.
Why This Still Matters
The danger here is not a stolen password - it is context. An attacker who knows a teacher’s or pupil’s email address and knows they use Bromcom can craft a convincing message: a fake “SSO re-registration” notice, a spoofed password reset, or a phishing page dressed up as a school IT request. Because the reference numbers look official, victims may treat the message as legitimate.
Pupil addresses raise a separate concern. Minors are a vulnerable population, and a confirmed link between a young person’s email and their school increases the risk of grooming, bullying, or targeted scams. Schools should treat this as a safeguarding matter, not just an IT one.
What to Do Right Now

Check your exposure. Visit haveibeenpwned.com/Breach/Bromcom and search your school email address. Staff should check work accounts; parents may wish to check addresses their children used.
Treat unexpected Bromcom emails with suspicion. Do not click links in messages asking you to “re-register,” “verify your SSO,” or “reset your password” unless you initiated the request and can confirm the sender.
Verify out of band. If you receive an IT-related email, contact your school’s IT desk directly using a known number, not a number in the message.
Enable multi-factor authentication on any Microsoft or Google account linked to your school identity. Bromcom says those accounts were not compromised, but MFA remains your best defence.
Watch for follow-up phishing. Expect messages that reference Bromcom by name or quote a reference number. Report them to your IT team.

Financial giants JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard have each acknowledged that customer data was compromised following security incidents at a common, but undisclosed, third-party vendor. The concurrent disclosures underscore the systemic risk posed by supply chain vulnerabilities in the Finance sector. The companies have asserted that these breaches are separate from other recent technology disruptions. This incident serves as a critical reminder that an organization's security posture is only as strong as its weakest link, and third-party risk management is paramount.

Threat Overview
The incident is a classic example of a Supply Chain Attack, where attackers target a larger organization by compromising one of its less secure partners or suppliers. Threat actors often find it easier to breach smaller vendors that may lack the robust security controls of a large financial institution. Once the vendor is compromised, attackers can access the sensitive data that the larger companies have entrusted to them.
The name of the compromised vendor and the specific nature of the breach have not been made public. Likewise, the full scope of the data exposure—including the number of affected customers and the specific data types stolen—has not been fully detailed. However, given the nature of the affected companies, the exposed data could potentially include customer names, account information, and other personally identifiable information (PII).
Technical Analysis
Without details on the specific vendor or attack vector, the technical analysis is based on common patterns for third-party breaches. The TTPs likely involved:

Initial Access (vs. Vendor): The attackers likely gained initial access to the third-party vendor's network through common methods such as phishing (T1566 - Phishing), exploiting an unpatched public-facing application (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application), or using stolen credentials.
Discovery (within Vendor): Once inside the vendor's network, the attackers would perform reconnaissance to locate the data belonging to JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard. This could involve searching for databases, file shares, or cloud storage buckets containing customer data (T1082 - System Information Discovery).
Collection: The attackers would then aggregate the target data from its various locations (T1005 - Data from Local System).
Exfiltration: Finally, the stolen data would be exfiltrated from the vendor's network to an attacker-controlled server (T1041 - Exfiltration Over C2 Channel).

The core technique from the perspective of the financial firms is Trusted Relationship (T1199), as they had granted the vendor access to their data, and the compromise of that trusted relationship led to the breach.
Impact Assessment
The impact of this breach could be significant, depending on the nature of the data exposed:

Fraud and Identity Theft: If customer PII and financial details were stolen, it could lead to a wave of fraud, identity theft, and targeted phishing attacks against the affected individuals.
Reputational Damage: Although the breach occurred at a third party, the brand names of JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard are associated with the incident, which can erode customer trust.

title: Fuite de données dans 43 caisses de crédit en Irlande
text:
Une faille chez Wellington IT a exposé des coordonnées bancaires de bénéficiaires enregistrés par des membres de caisses de crédit irlandaises. Le nombre de personnes touchées reste inconnu.
Quarante-trois coopératives de crédit irlandaises sont concernées par un incident chez Wellington IT, leur prestataire informatique basé à Belfast. L’enquête porte sur les fiches de bénéficiaires que les membres avaient enregistrées pour effectuer des virements. Selon les avis adressés aux clients, ces fiches peuvent contenir des IBAN, des noms et des références de paiement. Le fournisseur indique avoir corrigé la faille et n’avoir relevé aucun accès non autorisé aux fonds ni aucune activité frauduleuse sur les comptes. 1,8 million de personnes sont évoquées.
Une faille corrigée en octobre, des caisses alertées en novembre
Selon David Malone, directeur général de l’Irish League of Credit Unions (ILCU), le système a enregistré environ 1,4 million de tentatives d’activité entre le 2 et le 4 octobre 2026. Ce chiffre décrit l’activité observée sur la plateforme. Le nombre de fiches effectivement consultées ou copiées reste à établir. Wellington IT a corrigé la faille le 6 octobre à l’issue d’une évaluation de sécurité. La première enquête du fournisseur n’a toutefois pas détecté la possible fuite.
Wellington IT a identifié le risque pour les données le 15 novembre et informé les caisses le lendemain, d’après la chronologie rapportée par RTÉ. Le fournisseur dit avoir prévenu ses clients dès que ce risque a été établi et avoir fait appel à des spécialistes externes pour enquêter. Il transmet aux établissements concernés les informations dont il dispose sur les bénéficiaires touchés. Les représentants du secteur lui demandent de préciser combien de comptes et d’utilisateurs sont concernés.
La Commission irlandaise de protection des données a reçu plusieurs notifications de caisses et indiqué qu’elle prenait contact en priorité avec les parties concernées. Le ministère des Finances a échangé avec la Banque centrale d’Irlande pour évaluer les conséquences de l’incident. Le vice-Premier ministre et ministre des Finances, Simon Harris, a qualifié la situation de très préoccupante. Les établissements doivent informer directement leurs membres lorsque leurs obligations légales et réglementaires l’exigent.
Des fiches de bénéficiaires au cœur de l’enquête
Les avis consultés par BleepingComputer précisent la nature des données potentiellement exposées. Une fiche de bénéficiaire peut contenir le nom associé au compte destinataire, son IBAN, son code BIC ou ses coordonnées bancaires locales. Elle peut aussi inclure un surnom choisi par le membre, une adresse ou la référence saisie lors de l’enregistrement du bénéficiaire. Certains enregistrements peuvent révéler quel membre d’une caisse a sauvegardé la fiche. Le périmètre peut donc concerner à la fois les membres qui utilisent la plateforme et les personnes dont ils y ont enregistré les coordonnées.
Cette précision change la lecture de l’incident. L’enquête vise les données conservées pour préparer des virements. Les informations communiquées ne permettent pas d’établir qu’un historique complet des transactions a été consulté. Selon l’ILCU, les comptes et leurs soldes n’ont pas été compromis. Les avis aux membres indiquent également que les mots de passe, les codes PIN et les données de carte de paiement ont été épargnés.
L’association d’un nom, d’un IBAN et d’une référence de paiement présente néanmoins un risque d’hameçonnage ciblé. Une personne qui se fait passer pour un conseiller peut citer une information exacte pour rendre son appel crédible. Les associations professionnelles rappellent aux membres de garder leurs mots de passe, codes PIN et codes à usage unique confidentiels, y compris lorsqu’un interlocuteur affirme travailler pour leur caisse. Robert Troy, ministre délégué aux Finances, invite les membres qui s’interrogent sur leur situation à contacter directement leur établissement. […]

Directeur de l’IRIS

Le 19 novembre 2026, la Cour internationale de justice (CIJ) a reconnu la responsabilité du Myanmar dans le génocide contre la minorité rohingya. Une décision historique, qui soulève une question majeure : quelles implications ce jugement pourrait-il avoir dans la procédure engagée par l’Afrique du Sud contre Israël concernant Gaza ?

Les deux affaires présentent plusieurs similitudes : des persécutions menées à la suite d’attaques terroristes des groupes armés, des violences touchant principalement les civils, les femmes et les enfants, ainsi que la destruction des infrastructures et des ressources indispensables à la survie des populations. L’instrumentalisation des discours nationalistes et religieux constituent également un point de comparaison. Mais des différences importantes subsistent, notamment sur le plan politique : le Myanmar est dirigé par une junte militaire autoritaire, tandis qu’Israël est un État démocratique. Leurs situations diffèrent également quant aux possibilités de fuite des populations : la majorité des Rohingyas ont pu trouver refuge au Bangladesh, tandis que les Gazaouis restent largement contraints de demeurer dans la bande de Gaza.

Sept ans se sont écoulés entre le dépôt de la plainte de la Gambie contre le Myanmar et le jugement de la CIJ. À titre de comparaison, un calendrier similaire situerait une décision dans l’affaire Afrique du Sud c. Israël autour de 2030. Reste à savoir dans quelle mesure ce précédent historique constituera une référence juridique déterminante pour la CIJ dans l’examen de l’affaire Afrique du Sud c. Israël, notamment sur la question de l’intention génocidaire et de l’évaluation des preuves.

De l’influence à la manœuvre cognitive : le nouveau champ de bataille des armées françaises.

Alexandra Vilar

Publié le
23/11/2026

Analyse

Crédits : Éric Cadiou/ECPAD/Défense

6 min

À l’heure où l’ordre international vacille, la supériorité militaire ne se limite plus aux guerres conventionnelles. Du traumatisme sahélien à la guerre en Ukraine, l’armée française a beaucoup évolué. Désormais, l’institution militaire considère l’influence comme un véritable champ de lutte. Cette approche s’impose au sein des cellules de prospective d’anticipation et de stratégie à l’État-Major de l’Armée de terre (EMAT) à Balard. Elle s’inscrit dans un contexte marqué par l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle.

« Quel sera le monde lorsque nous aurons digéré l’intelligence artificielle et le quantique ? » Au sein de l’État-Major des Armées, cette question résulte des dynamiques et des mutations du contexte international.

La Revue nationale stratégique de 2025 dresse un constat clair sur l’état du monde. L’environnement international est à l’agonie, et les menaces qui pèsent sur l’Europe sont beaucoup plus présentes. Les armées françaises doivent se préparer à la guerre de haute intensité. De plus, elles doivent intégrer les défis structurels majeurs, comme le changement climatique et la démographie. Le Chef d’État-Major des Armées, l’a d’ailleurs souligné le 18 novembre 2025.

De son côté, l’association Paroles de défense a organisé une conférence à l’université Paris-Panthéon-Assas. Elle portait sur l’influence et la lutte informationnelle comme nouveau domaine de lutte des armées françaises. Le général de division Ivan Martin y a souligné les profondes transformations qui redessinent le cadre stratégique des armées. Face au retour de la guerre en Europe, à l’instabilité géopolitique et aux menaces hybrides, l’enjeu est désormais clair. Il s’agit pour les armées de bâtir une stratégie d’influence concrète. L’influence et la lutte informationnelle ne sont plus de simples fonctions d’appui : elles sont désormais un domaine de lutte stratégique.

La guerre informationnelle à l’épreuve de l’influence et du champ cognitif

La première difficulté des stratèges réside dans la définition du concept. L’influence militaire a longtemps suivi le modèle du Soft Power, théorisé par Joseph Nye. Elle s’exprimait sans audience spécifique et s’appuyait sur les outils traditionnels de l’État. Ce qui inclut des partenariats de défense, la diplomatique à l’étranger ou l’accueil des élèves étrangers au sein des écoles militaires françaises. Cette approche reposait sur une logique naturelle de la France : ce qu’elle est, fait et représente.

Aujourd’hui, le changement de paradigme est total. L’influence militaire devient une véritable manœuvre visant à produire des effets cognitifs mesurables. Elle s’appuie sur un flux permanent de contenus et regroupe l’ensemble des activités planifiées domaine militaire. À la fois offensives et défensives, ces actions visent  à influencer les perceptions et à modifier les attitudes ciblées. Elles restent largement invisibles pour le grand public à cause de leur sensibilité opérationnelle. Elles font malgré tout l’objet d’une prise en compte prioritaire au plus haut sommet de l’institution.

La confrontation informationnelle entre puissance : l’électrochoc du Sahel

La fin de l’opération Barkhane en 2022 et le retrait des troupes françaises du Sahel mettent en évidence l’efficacité des manœuvres informationnelles russes. Ces actions mettent en évidence la fragilité d’un acteur dans le cadre d’une guerre des perceptions. Grâce à ses stratégies d’influence, la Russie a durablement fragilisé la présence française et sa coopération sécuritaire en Afrique.

title: Same Risk, Different Letterhead? The City Watchdog Takes On the Professions
text: City watchdog, the Financial Conduct Authority is taking on the professions able to enable money-laundering.Decisions remain as the UK debates a Bill on anti-money laundering supervision of lawyers, accountants and company formation agents to the Financial Conduct Authority.It is hard – very hard – for criminals, terrorists or hostile states to move dirty money without a professional somewhere in the chain. When a sanctioned oligarch’s London townhouse changes hands through an offshore company, a formation agent registers the company, a solicitor conveys the house, and an accountant keeps the books. Anti-money laundering (AML) supervision ensures these professionals ask the right questions and refuse the wrong clients.In the UK, that job falls to a crowd – 22 professional bodies, from the Bar Council to the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales – and HMRC (HM Revenue and Customs) for the rest. Every official verdict on these arrangements over the past decade has been unfavourable, and in 2018 the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global standard setter against money laundering, agreed. An overseer within the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Office for Professional Body Anti-Money Laundering Supervision (OPBAS), has helped since 2018, but progress has been limited.In October 2025, the government chose radical change, moving AML supervision of the professions to the FCA alone. The Financial Services and Markets Bill, which gives effect to it, has cleared the Lords, and on Tuesday 10 November, MPs gave it a second reading. It will pass, and it should; consolidation is the right call.quoteBut a Bill that moves firms from one group of supervisors to another will, on its own, only change a letterhead But a Bill that moves firms from one group of supervisors to another will, on its own, only change a letterhead. As a forthcoming RUSI Insights Paper, Reforming UK Anti-Money Laundering Supervision of the Professions, argues, it will not change the risks or improve supervision. In fairness to the government, detailed mechanics belong to the regulations that will follow, but peers and MPs have pressed ministers on exactly these gaps.Rejecting ‘One-Size-Fits-All’Much is already settled. Some 60,000 firms will move: 34,000 accountancy and 7,500 law firms supervised by the professional bodies, and 18,000 accountancy firms and company formation agents by HMRC, from City firms to sole practitioners. The FCA will supervise them under the money laundering regulations (MLRs). Every firm will register with the FCA, and the ‘fit and proper’ test that now vets only the owners and managers of formation agents will extend to law and accountancy firms. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.
The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.
Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations
To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received
Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials
Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”
Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router to another one. Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

Debian 13.8 bundles kernel and Chromium security fixes with a 122-package bugfix list

The Debian project released Debian 13.8, the eighth update to its stable “trixie” series. It mainly carries security fixes, plus corrections for a few serious bugs, and it bundles advisories Debian had already published separately.

ClamAV, the open-source antivirus scanner, moved to a new upstream stable release with fixes for 13 CVEs. Other packages got smaller repairs: build failures, Thunderbird 153 compatibility and updated tzdata time zone data.
Existing installs get 13.8 by upgrading packages from an HTTP mirror, and old trixie install media still works. If you already pull updates from security.debian.org often, you will find few packages left to update, since most of those fixes are already in the release.

Black Friday scams started earlier this year without the usual red flags

This year’s fake Black Friday deals started appearing on September 1, more than a month earlier than last year, and most of them don’t mention the holiday or use a lookalike address, according to Doppel.
The company describes the lure most shoppers are likely to meet this season as “a post in a Facebook group or a page on Google Sites, carrying a retailer’s sale language on behalf of a software, payment, travel, or crypto brand, and asking for a login.”
Facebook groups carry the bulk of it
Half of the confirmed social media brand impersonation Doppel tracked between September 1 and late October was posted inside Facebook groups, and 99.7% of confirmed fraudulent ads ran on Facebook Ads.
Bargain and buy-and-sell groups are where people go hunting for discounts, and Doppel says a scam post in one of them “carries the group’s implied vetting.”

Source: Doppel

Checking the address won’t help
Looking for the brand’s name in the web address is the one habit most shoppers have, and Doppel found it “passes most of this season’s confirmed fake pages.”
About one in four lookalike pages are hosted on legitimate platforms such as Google Sites, Blogger and GitHub Pages, and those with their own domain tend to use a generic deal or outlet term while the brand’s logo appears on the page.
More than a third of these sites are built to steal logins to accounts visitors already hold. About a third also cloak, so “a scanner, a reviewer, or a brand’s own staff can see something harmless while a shopper in the target market sees the lure.” One holiday sale scam showed its checkout only to visitors on phones.
Software and travel brands lead the target list
Retailers made up under a tenth of confirmed sale-themed lookalikes in 2025 and about a tenth so far this year. Last season, airlines were the biggest target through discount and deal pages, followed by crypto exchanges and neobanks. In 2026 business software has taken the top spot, with travel, crypto, retail and payment brands behind it.
“A holiday discount is a credible pretext for any brand a shopper has an account with,” researchers explained.
Travel scams have also picked up the holiday name. Most of the Black Friday-named hosts Doppel confirmed between September 1 and October 15 posed as travel fare or booking pages, while no travel page with Black Friday in its address turned up in either of the two previous seasons. Travel is an expensive purchase that people tend to make quickly when a fare looks like it might disappear, and “the holiday supplies the scarcity,” the analysts wrote.
Cyber Monday, on the other hand, hasn’t appeared in the address of a single confirmed lookalike aimed at a Doppel-protected brand in three holiday seasons. “When actors name the holiday, they name Black Friday.”
The company also found that a quarter of confirmed brand impersonation texts were delivered through iMessage and RCS, which SMS spam filters don’t cover.
“A security leader at a brand that never runs a sale now has a Black Friday problem, because the lure does not care whether the brand sells anything,” Doppel concluded.

A large malvertising campaign spent roughly six months turning ordinary online ads into a delivery system for iPhone exploits. The target was crypto wallet seed phrases.
Cybersecurity firm Confiant laid out the operation, which it calls MoldyRoost, in a report dated November 20, 2026. The uncomfortable twist is that victims did not need to download anything or tap through a sketchy prompt. Landing on the wrong page was enough.

How MoldyRoost worked
According to Confiant, MoldyRoost ran through programmatic ads. These are the automated auctions that decide which banner you see on a webpage in a fraction of a second.
The campaign was active from May 12 to November 17, 2026. Over that window, Confiant tied more than 480 ad domains to six sub-clusters of activity.
One cluster dominated. It contained 403 domains and focused mainly on Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore, though the broader operation reached iPhones across 47 countries.
The technical payload is where things get serious. MoldyRoost deployed 23 exploits arranged into five chains aimed at iOS versions 13 through 17.2.1.

It also carried six additional vulnerabilities for iOS 18.4 through 18.7. Three of those were zero-days, meaning flaws that had no available fix at the time they were used.
The exploit families involved include ones known as Coruna and DarkSword. Taken together, the toolkit covered 29 vulnerabilities across older iOS releases.

Once inside a device, the malware went looking for recovery phrases tied to popular wallets, including MetaMask, Phantom, and Trust Wallet. It searched Notes, images, messages, and keychain data.
Why the drive-by angle matters
MoldyRoost skipped that step entirely. Confiant describes the attacks as drive-by: the exploit chain fired automatically once a user visited the malicious landing page.
It is worth being precise about where the weakness lived. The vulnerabilities sat in Apple’s iOS operating system, not in the wallet apps themselves. MetaMask, Phantom, and Trust Wallet were targets because of what users stored around them, not because of a flaw in their code.
The good news for updated iPhones
Researchers found no confirmed exploit code for iOS 26. Apple also patched the vulnerabilities associated with DarkSword in iOS 26.3 while the operation was still running.
Confiant’s findings show no evidence of these exploits succeeding on fully updated devices running iOS 26.
What this means for crypto holders
A seed phrase is the master key to a self-custody wallet. Anyone holding those words can move the funds, and blockchain transactions generally cannot be reversed.
Storing a recovery phrase in Notes or a photo album effectively ties the safety of your crypto to the security of your entire operating system. When that operating system has a zero-day, your wallet inherits the problem.
The regional focus also matters. The largest cluster concentrated on Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore, all markets with active crypto user bases.
The practical checklist is short. Update iOS to the latest version, move any recovery phrase off the device entirely, and treat a phone’s photo library as a place where secrets are never truly private.

Infected TV boxes in BADBOX 3.0 rent out their owners’ home internet

HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team has disrupted BADBOX 3.0, an operation run mainly from infected low-cost TV boxes that generated roughly 40 billion ad bid requests a day at its peak. That was more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic HUMAN observed and more than three times the volume of VASTFLUX, the previous record holder.
The boxes play video ads in a window the owner never sees, and the requests claim to come from well-known streaming apps that do not run on the device.
The same boxes also rent out the owner’s home internet connection to residential proxy networks, which threat actors use to make attacks look like household traffic. Advertisers may pay for ads that no one watches, and the people guarding accounts and payments may see takeover or carding attempts arriving from what looks like a living room.
BADBOX, found in 2023, was a firmware backdoor on uncertified devices, and HUMAN observed more than 74,000 of them. BADBOX 2.0, in 2025, spanned more than 10 million devices in 222 countries and territories. The 3.0 operators reuse pieces of both, including a proxy network first exposed in 2.0.
A catalog hosted in the open
Infected devices contact a command-and-control server, which returns a list of fraud modules and where to download them. The modules sit on public code repositories, with backups on a second code platform, an operator-controlled file server and, for some, a CDN mirror. The operators also run their own GitHub proxy, so blocking the repositories at the network level does not stop the downloads.
One month of CDN statistics for a single repository showed 367,023 requests and about 482.7 GB served. Those are requests, not unique devices, and cover one repository and one of four delivery routes, so Satori presumes actual infections are significantly higher. Antivirus coverage of the newer modules was effectively absent at the time of analysis.
Ads that look like premium inventory
The ad modules mimic legitimate video ad software and render the ads in a hidden window. To a buyer, the request looks like a well-known app, a residential IP address and a full video ad. The apps sending the requests have no business relationship with the apps they claim to be and do not appear in those apps’ sellers.json or app-ads.txt files, where such files exist.
The traffic still has tells. For one abused app identity, about 40% of requests overall and 80% of US requests came from residential proxy exits. A small set of cheap, uncertified Android device models sent nearly all requests to one family of apps, while ordinary CTV devices spread theirs across many.
Eleven proxy networks
Other modules enroll devices in eleven residential proxy networks: ten commercial services and PXYEDGE, which Satori assesses to be IpMoYu, the network exposed in BADBOX 2.0, under a new name. The PXYEDGE domain was registered March 15, 2026, and reports about 200,000 nodes. The owner pays for the bandwidth while someone else sells access to the address.
A Chinese manufacturer is linked
Satori ties the catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer. Modules check for TXCZ-specific build properties before running, and a TXCZ launcher with system-level permissions comes preinstalled on its devices.
